item.title: 🔵 As phishing-as-a-service goes industrial, Microsoft takes down a marketplace behind 1 billion messages
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Microsoft says it has dismantled a criminal marketplace responsible for 1 billion malicious messages.

Working with international authorities and several tech and cybersecurity companies in a nearly year-long investigation, Redmond identified and took down Yam Store, a coordinated underground network dealing in commercial phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS).

The network allowed cybercriminals to readily purchase, and very quickly deploy, pre-made kits they could use in phishing attacks to steal data and credentials.

Microsoft said the takedown began as a simple investigation based on a tip from Japanese authorities.

item.title: 🟠 MCP is changing the questions marketers can afford to ask
item.description:
Why this matters: Compliance/regulatory signal — determine applicability and required action.

Picture a regional marketing director on a Monday morning. She’s got 80 locations, a cup of coffee, and a nagging feeling that something is off in the Southeast. Reviews seem quieter. A couple of stores got new managers last month. Are those two things related?

Not long ago, finding out meant pulling an export, building a pivot table, pulling a second export from another system, and stitching it all together in a spreadsheet. Or, more realistically, filing a request with an analyst and waiting. Most weeks, the question simply never got asked.

Now she types it into the AI assistant her company already rolled out, and it answers using live data from the systems where that data actually lives.

The technology making that possible is the Model Context Protocol, or MCP. You’ve probably read plenty of “what is MCP” explainers by now, so I won’t add another. Instead, I want to talk about what changes for marketing teams, especially those managing lots of locations, when a cross-system question gets this cheap to ask. And what CIOs need to get right before it…

item.title: 🔵 Human in the loop is an engineering problem
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

A customer leaves a one-star review at one of your locations. An AI drafts a reply in seconds. It’s warm, on-brand, grammatically perfect, and it thanks the customer for their feedback and invites them back soon.

The review was about a customer who slipped and was hurt in the parking lot.

Nothing in that reply is factually false. It would pass a spell-checker, a brand-voice check, and probably a quick skim from a busy manager. It’s still the wrong answer, and if it goes out publicly, it’s the kind of wrong that ends up in a screenshot.

I spend most of my time building systems that put AI to work on reputation data: reviews, listings, surveys, and the replies and summaries generated from them. The most important lesson I’ve learned is that “human in the loop” is an engineering problem. Where the human sits, what they see, what gets routed to them and what doesn’t—all of that is system design.

Get it right, and AI can move fast without embarrassing you. Get it wrong, and you either drown your reviewers or give them…

item.title: 🟠 Beyond the perimeter: The network as the security fabric for the AI era
item.description:
Why this matters: Potential data exposure — review monitoring and incident-response readiness.

Enterprises have historically built separate network and security architectures, but this separation is becoming increasingly difficult to maintain as frontier AI models mature and security architectures shift from perimeter-based defenses to identity- and context-aware enforcement.

Frontier AI does not change existing cybersecurity fundamentals; it narrows the time available to apply them. As attacks move from human speed to machine speed, enterprises need security controls that can detect, respond, and enforce at the same speed. The network is uniquely positioned to become that enforcement and containment fabric.

The AI era requires enterprises to treat the network as an active security control, not simply as infrastructure to be protected. By integrating identity, telemetry, segmentation, and automated enforcement, the network can reduce exposure, contain compromise, and accelerate recovery at machine speed.

item.title: 🟠 Unplug your smart fridges, French supermarkets warned after cyberattack
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

More internet-connected refrigerators have joined the official list of those affected by a cyberattack that ruined stocks of chilled food at hundreds of French supermarkets over the weekend.

The French Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-FR) advised supermarkets to disconnect any refrigeration control systems with a public IP address from the internet, and to reconnect them via a secure VPN only after verifying the configuration and, if necessary, restoring factory defaults.

In an emergency, it suggested, they could simply filter connections to allow only the IP addresses of their refrigeration suppliers or service providers to connect, but this should not be a long-term solution, CERT-FR said.

CERT-FR’s initial warning on Monday listed only Danfoss AK-SC and AK-SM series refrigeration controllers as affected, advising supermarkets to update the firmware of their systems, set the security level to “strict,” and ensure that default passwords had been changed.

item.description:

There is a lot of discussion about deploying AI across the enterprise. Most of it starts with the model, the platform or the tool. I start somewhere else: the work.

What decision are we trying to improve? What information does a person need at that moment? What gets in the way today? And what should the technology do when the situation does not fit the standard process? Those questions matter whether the employee is working at a desk, supporting a customer, writing software or managing a shift.

The work is different across those environments, but the technology challenge is connected. AI creates value when it is grounded in the context of the work and built into the workflow. It does not create value simply because it has been deployed.

Companies are moving fast to put AI into chatbots, virtual assistants, and other customer service tools. But for CIOs, that comes with a risk: if the technology gives customers the wrong information, makes biased recommendations, or mishandles data, it can immediately damage the trust companies have worked hard to build.

Unlike conventional software, gen AI doesn’t always give the same answer to the same question. An answer can sound confident and convincing while still wrong. And when customers rely on AI for information about their finances, insurance, or health, a mistake can have much greater consequences.

Sumit Johar, CIO at cloud-based software company BlackLine, understands that inaccurate AI responses hurt the customer experience, force companies to spend money and resources to fix problems, damage the brand, and create regulatory risks. item.title: 🟠 AI is changing (and chaining) the cybersecurity math
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

For years, cybersecurity teams have worked from a relatively straightforward model: identify the critical vulnerability, patch it and reduce the risk.  That model still matters, but it is no longer enough.

The growing concern is not simply that attackers can use AI to write better phishing emails or generate malicious code faster. The bigger issue is that AI can help adversaries connect seemingly benign vulnerabilities into an attack path that security teams may never have considered.

A low-severity application flaw, exposed API, over-permissioned service account, cloud misconfiguration and AI agent with excessive access may not be alarming individually. But when they can be identified, sequenced and exploited together, they can create a serious breach.

This is the new cybersecurity challenge: AI-enabled vulnerability service chaining.

item.title: 🔴 Cybersecurity is a leadership problem: Why the management model needs to catch up
item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

When I started writing regularly about cybersecurity management in 2015, the environment looked very different.

Cloud computing was still reshaping enterprise technology. Ransomware had not become the industrialised threat it is today. Artificial intelligence was not driving boardroom discussions. Zero Trust had yet to enter mainstream technical vocabulary and quantum computing barely registered on the corporate risk horizon.

Cybersecurity itself also occupied a different position. The CISO role was less established, board engagement was inconsistent, regulation was less extensive and security budgets were generally smaller.

Much has changed since then.

But looking back at the management challenges we were discussing more than a decade ago raises an uncomfortable question:

Why are we still discussing so many of them?

item.title: 🔵 6 IT wins to deliver before the year ends
item.description:
Why this matters: Hospitality-system impact — consider guest services, PMS/POS, and property operations.

CIOs entered the year with ambitions to bring more AI into their companies and start using AI to transform how work gets done. At the same time they also wanted to leverage tech to cut costs and boost productivity throughout the business. And they hoped to use their post to help drive the strategic vision for their organizations.
